1. When the Sun Throws a Tantrum

On October 28, 2003, the Sun threw a tantrum so violent it rewrote the textbooks. A colossal X17.2 flare, one of the most powerful ever recorded, erupted from sunspot region 486, hurling a wall of magnetized plasma toward Earth at over 2,000 km/s. Within hours, airline flights were rerouted over the poles, satellites tumbled out of orientation, and the Swedish power grid went dark. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station retreated to shielded modules. Auroras, normally confined to the Arctic, painted the skies as far south as Florida and Texas.

That week, known as the Halloween Solar Storms, was not an anomaly. It was a reminder: our star is not the calm, steady lantern it appears to be. It breathes, it cycles, it rages, and our increasingly electrified civilization sits squarely in the blast zone.

This notebook explores 27 years of space weather data (1997–2024), spanning nearly three complete solar cycles. We will trace the Sun’s heartbeat through sunspot counts and radio flux, decode the geomagnetic tremors it sends rippling through Earth’s magnetosphere, and hunt for the patterns that connect solar fury to terrestrial disruption.

NoteWhat is Space Weather?

Space weather describes the conditions in the space environment between the Sun and Earth. It is driven by the Sun’s magnetic activity and affects:

  • Satellite operations, charged particles degrade solar panels and corrupt electronics
  • GPS and communications, ionospheric disturbances cause positioning errors and radio blackouts
  • Power grids, geomagnetically induced currents can overload transformers (the 1989 Quebec blackout left 6 million people without power for 9 hours)
  • Astronaut safety, solar energetic particles pose a serious radiation hazard
  • Aviation, high-latitude flights receive increased radiation doses during solar storms

Understanding space weather is not just academic curiosity, it is critical infrastructure protection.

Loading and Cleaning the Data

Code 
# Download dataset from Kaggle
path = kagglehub.dataset_download("erevear/space-weather-solar-geomagnetic-indices")

# Load both CSV files
solar_raw = pd.read_csv(f"{path}/daily_solar_data.csv")
geo_raw = pd.read_csv(f"{path}/daily_geomagnetic_data.csv")

print(f"Solar data (raw):        {solar_raw.shape[0]:,} rows x {solar_raw.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"Geomagnetic data (raw):  {geo_raw.shape[0]:,} rows x {geo_raw.shape[1]} columns")
Solar data (raw):        10,330 rows x 14 columns
Geomagnetic data (raw):  78,672 rows x 7 columns
Code 
# --- Solar data cleaning ---
solar = solar_raw.copy()

# Drop duplicate dates (457 duplicates from 2017-2018)
solar = solar.drop_duplicates(subset="Date", keep="first").reset_index(drop=True)

# Parse dates
solar["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(solar["Date"])

# Replace sentinels with NaN
for col in solar.columns:
    if solar[col].dtype == object and col != "Date":
        solar[col] = solar[col].replace("*", np.nan)
        solar[col] = pd.to_numeric(solar[col], errors="coerce")

# -999 sentinel in Stanford fields, -1 in flare columns
stanford_cols = [c for c in solar.columns if "Stanford" in c]
solar[stanford_cols] = solar[stanford_cols].replace(-999, np.nan)

flare_cols = [c for c in solar.columns if "Flares" in c]
solar[flare_cols] = solar[flare_cols].replace(-1, np.nan)

# Ensure all numeric columns are proper numeric types
for col in [c for c in solar.columns if c != "Date"]:
    solar[col] = pd.to_numeric(solar[col], errors="coerce")

# --- Geomagnetic data cleaning ---
geo = geo_raw.copy()

# Drop duplicate timestamps (7264 duplicates)
geo = geo.drop_duplicates(subset="Timestamp", keep="first").reset_index(drop=True)

# Parse timestamps and replace sentinels
geo["Timestamp"] = pd.to_datetime(geo["Timestamp"])

for col in geo.columns:
    if geo[col].dtype == object and col != "Timestamp":
        geo[col] = geo[col].replace("*", np.nan)
        geo[col] = pd.to_numeric(geo[col], errors="coerce")

for col in [c for c in geo.columns if c != "Timestamp"]:
    geo[col] = pd.to_numeric(geo[col], errors="coerce")
    geo[col] = geo[col].replace(-1, np.nan)

# Create date column for daily aggregation
geo["Date"] = geo["Timestamp"].dt.normalize()

# A-indices: daily (repeated 8x) -> take first
# K-indices: true 3-hourly -> compute mean and max per day
a_cols = ["Middle Latitude A", "High Latitude A", "Estimated A"]
k_cols = ["Middle Latitude K", "High Latitude K", "Estimated K"]

geo_a = geo.groupby("Date")[a_cols].first().reset_index()
geo_k_mean = geo.groupby("Date")[k_cols].mean().reset_index()
geo_k_mean.columns = ["Date"] + [f"{c} Mean" for c in k_cols]
geo_k_max = geo.groupby("Date")[k_cols].max().reset_index()
geo_k_max.columns = ["Date"] + [f"{c} Max" for c in k_cols]

geo_daily = geo_a.merge(geo_k_mean, on="Date").merge(geo_k_max, on="Date")

# --- Merge solar + geomagnetic on Date ---
df = solar.merge(geo_daily, on="Date", how="inner")
df = df.sort_values("Date").reset_index(drop=True)

print(f"\nAfter cleaning:")
print(f"  Solar:        {solar.shape[0]:,} rows x {solar.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"  Geomagnetic:  {geo_daily.shape[0]:,} rows x {geo_daily.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"  Merged:       {df.shape[0]:,} rows x {df.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"  Date range:   {df['Date'].min().strftime('%Y-%m-%d')} to {df['Date'].max().strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}")

After cleaning:
  Solar:        9,873 rows x 14 columns
  Geomagnetic:  9,380 rows x 10 columns
  Merged:       9,293 rows x 23 columns
  Date range:   1997-01-01 to 2024-04-12
TipKey Space Weather Indices

The dataset tracks several complementary measures of solar and geomagnetic activity:

Solar indices:

  • Sunspot Number (SSN), a count of dark, magnetically active spots on the Sun’s visible disk. More sunspots = more active Sun. The primary tracker of the ~11-year solar cycle.
  • F10.7 Radio Flux, solar radio emission at 10.7 cm wavelength (2800 MHz), measured in Solar Flux Units (SFU). Correlates tightly with sunspot number but can be measured through clouds and at night.
  • Solar Flares (C / M / X), sudden bursts of electromagnetic radiation, classified on a logarithmic scale: C-class (minor), M-class (moderate, 10x C), X-class (extreme, 10x M). An X10 flare is 1,000x more powerful than a C1.

Geomagnetic indices:

  • K-index (Kp), a quasi-logarithmic 0–9 scale measuring geomagnetic disturbance over 3-hour intervals. K >= 5 indicates a geomagnetic storm.
  • A-index (Ap), a daily linearized equivalent of the K-index. Ap >= 50 signals a significant storm; Ap >= 100 is severe.

2. The Solar Heartbeat: 11-Year Cycles

The Sun is not a static ball of fire, it is a churning, magnetized dynamo with a pulse. Roughly every 11 years, the Sun’s magnetic field undergoes a dramatic reversal: its north and south magnetic poles flip. This magnetic cycle drives the rise and fall of sunspot activity, flare frequency, and coronal mass ejections.

Our dataset spans the tail end of Solar Cycle 23 (which peaked around 2000–2002), the entirety of the unusually weak Cycle 24 (peak ~2014), and the ascending phase of Cycle 25 (currently underway, with activity ramping up sharply since 2022).

NoteWhy 11 Years?

The solar cycle is driven by the Sun’s differential rotation, the equator rotates faster than the poles. This shearing motion stretches and tangles the Sun’s magnetic field lines over time, building up magnetic stress. Sunspots emerge where tangled magnetic flux tubes break through the surface.

After roughly 11 years, the accumulated tangling causes the global magnetic field to reverse polarity (north becomes south). The full magnetic cycle is actually 22 years, it takes two reversals to return to the original configuration, but the 11-year activity cycle is what we observe most directly.

Cycle 24 (2008–2019) was notably weaker than its predecessors, leading some solar physicists to speculate about a possible grand minimum. Cycle 25, however, has exceeded all predictions and is shaping up to be significantly stronger than Cycle 24.

Code 
# Assign solar cycle labels
def assign_cycle(date):
    if date < pd.Timestamp("2008-12-01"):
        return "Cycle 23"
    elif date < pd.Timestamp("2019-12-01"):
        return "Cycle 24"
    else:
        return "Cycle 25"

df["Solar Cycle"] = df["Date"].apply(assign_cycle)

# Yearly average sunspot number
yearly = df.groupby([df["Date"].dt.year, "Solar Cycle"]).agg(
    SSN_mean=("Sunspot Number", "mean")
).reset_index()
yearly.columns = ["Year", "Solar Cycle", "SSN_mean"]

cycle_colors = {"Cycle 23": SOLAR_PRIMARY, "Cycle 24": SOLAR_SECONDARY, "Cycle 25": ALERT_COLOR}

fig_yearly = go.Figure()
for cycle in ["Cycle 23", "Cycle 24", "Cycle 25"]:
    mask = yearly["Solar Cycle"] == cycle
    fig_yearly.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=yearly.loc[mask, "Year"], y=yearly.loc[mask, "SSN_mean"],
        name=cycle, marker_color=cycle_colors[cycle],
        hovertemplate="Year: %{x}<br>Mean SSN: %{y:.1f}<extra>" + cycle + "</extra>",
    ))

fig_yearly.update_layout(
    title="Yearly Average Sunspot Number by Solar Cycle",
    xaxis_title="Year", yaxis_title="Mean Daily Sunspot Number",
    height=420, margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=50, b=40),
    barmode="stack",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.2, xanchor="center", x=0.5),
    yaxis_rangemode="tozero",
)
fig_yearly.show()

The cyclic pattern is unmistakable. Each cycle rises over ~4 years, peaks, then declines over ~7 years. Notice how Cycle 24’s peak (annual mean SSN around 80–110) was roughly half the amplitude of Cycle 23, and how Cycle 25 has already surpassed Cycle 24’s maximum, defying the conservative forecasts issued at its onset.

3. The Sun-Earth Connection: Multi-Variable Correlation

Solar activity does not happen in isolation. A burst of X-ray flares on the Sun’s surface can trigger a cascade that reaches Earth within minutes (electromagnetic radiation) to days (coronal mass ejections). But how tightly are these phenomena coupled in the data?

Code 
# Correlation heatmap
corr_cols = [
    "Sunspot Number", "Radio Flux 10.7cm", "Sunspot Area (10^6 Hemis.)",
    "Flares: C", "Flares: M", "Flares: X",
    "Estimated A", "Estimated K Mean",
]
corr_labels = ["Sunspot Number", "F10.7 Flux", "Sunspot Area",
               "Flares C", "Flares M", "Flares X", "A-index", "K Mean"]

corr_matrix = df[corr_cols].corr(method="pearson")

space_colorscale = [

    [0.5, "#f5f5f5"], [0.75, "#ffb899"], [1.0, SOLAR_PRIMARY],
]

z_text = [[f"{val:.2f}" for val in row] for row in corr_matrix.values]

fig_corr = go.Figure(data=go.Heatmap(
    z=corr_matrix.values, x=corr_labels, y=corr_labels,
    colorscale=space_colorscale, zmin=-1, zmax=1,
    text=z_text, texttemplate="%{text}", textfont=dict(size=11),
    hovertemplate="(%{x}, %{y})<br>r = %{z:.3f}<extra></extra>",

    height=550, width=680,

    yaxis=dict(autorange="reversed"),
)
fig_corr.show()
NoteCorrelation Is Not Causation, But Here, the Physics Is Clear

In most datasets, we caution against interpreting correlation as causation. Space weather is one of the rare domains where the causal chain is unambiguous and well-understood:

  1. Magnetic dynamo in the Sun’s interior generates sunspots and active regions
  2. Active regions produce solar flares (C, M, X-class) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs)
  3. Flares emit X-rays and UV radiation that disturb Earth’s ionosphere within 8 minutes
  4. CMEs launch magnetized plasma that impacts Earth’s magnetosphere 1–3 days later
  5. Magnetospheric compression drives geomagnetic storms measured by K and A indices

Three stories emerge:

  • SSN vs F10.7 Flux shows a remarkably tight linear relationship, these two indices are nearly interchangeable proxies for solar activity.
  • X-class Flares vs K Mean reveals a weaker but meaningful link between extreme solar events and geomagnetic disturbance. The scatter is wide because not every flare produces an Earth-directed CME.
  • SSN vs A-index shows a positive but diffuse relationship, mediated by the solar wind, a complex, turbulent intermediary.

4. Solar Flares and Geomagnetic Impact

Solar flares are classified on a logarithmic scale based on their peak X-ray flux in the 1–8 Angstrom band. Each class represents a tenfold increase in energy:

Class Peak Flux (W/m2) Typical Effects
C 10-6 – 10-5 Minor; few noticeable consequences
M 10-5 – 10-4 Moderate; brief radio blackouts at poles
X > 10-4 Major; wide-area radio blackouts, radiation storms

When a flare is accompanied by a Coronal Mass Ejection (CME), the ejected plasma compresses our magnetosphere, producing geomagnetic storms. The critical question: how long after a flare do we see the geomagnetic response?

The Sun-to-Earth Delay

When an X-class flare erupts, how quickly does Earth feel the geomagnetic effects? Let’s measure this delay empirically with a superposed epoch analysis, averaging Kp around all X-flare days.

Code 
# Superposed epoch analysis: Kp around X-flare days
x_flare_days = df.loc[df["Flares: X"] > 0, "Date"].values

window = range(-3, 4)
epoch_data = {day_offset: [] for day_offset in window}

for flare_date in x_flare_days:
    for offset in window:
        target_date = flare_date + np.timedelta64(offset, "D")
        match = df.loc[df["Date"] == target_date, "Estimated K Max"]
        if len(match) == 1 and not np.isnan(match.values[0]):
            epoch_data[offset].append(match.values[0])

offsets = list(window)
means = [np.mean(epoch_data[o]) if epoch_data[o] else np.nan for o in offsets]
stderrs = [np.std(epoch_data[o]) / np.sqrt(len(epoch_data[o])) if len(epoch_data[o]) > 1 else 0 for o in offsets]

upper = [m + 1.96 * s for m, s in zip(means, stderrs)]
lower = [m - 1.96 * s for m, s in zip(means, stderrs)]

fig_epoch = go.Figure()

# Confidence band
fig_epoch.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=offsets + offsets[::-1], y=upper + lower[::-1],
    fill="toself", fillcolor="rgba(239,71,111,0.15)",
    line=dict(color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"), showlegend=False, name="95% CI",
))

# Mean line
fig_epoch.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=offsets, y=means, mode="lines+markers",
    line=dict(color=ALERT_COLOR, width=3),
    marker=dict(size=10, color=ALERT_COLOR), name="Mean Kp (max)",
))

fig_epoch.add_shape(
    type="line", x0=0, x1=0, y0=0, y1=1, yref="paper",
    line=dict(color=NEUTRAL, width=1.5, dash="dash"),
)
fig_epoch.add_annotation(
    x=0, y=1.05, yref="paper", text="Flare day",
    showarrow=False, font=dict(size=11, color=NEUTRAL),
)

fig_epoch.update_layout(
    title="Superposed Epoch Analysis: Kp Response to X-class Flares",
    xaxis_title="Days Relative to X-class Flare",
    yaxis_title="Average Estimated Kp (max)",
    height=450,
)
fig_epoch.show()

The superposed epoch analysis reveals the expected pattern: Kp tends to peak 1–2 days after an X-class flare, consistent with CME transit times.

The violin plots show a clear upward shift: days with M-class and X-class flares tend to have higher Kp values, though the overlap is substantial, not every powerful flare produces a geomagnetic storm.

TipCME Travel Time

A Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) is a massive expulsion of magnetised plasma from the solar corona. Typical CME speeds range from 400 to 2000+ km/s. At these speeds, the Sun-Earth distance of ~150 million km is covered in:

  • Slow CME (~400 km/s): ~4 days
  • Average CME (~800 km/s): ~2 days
  • Fast CME (~2000 km/s): ~18 hours

This is why we observe a 1–3 day lag between a solar flare and the onset of a geomagnetic storm.

5. Anomaly Detection: Finding Extreme Space Weather

Extreme space weather events are rare but consequential. The Carrington Event of 1859 remains the most powerful recorded geomagnetic storm, if it happened today, it could cause trillions of dollars in damage. Can we systematically detect anomalous days in our dataset?

We compare two approaches: a classical statistical method (IQR) and a machine learning method (Isolation Forest).

5.1 IQR Method (Statistical Baseline)

Code 
# IQR-based anomaly detection
def iqr_anomalies(series, factor=1.5):
    """Flag values above Q3 + factor * IQR as anomalies."""
    q1, q3 = series.quantile(0.25), series.quantile(0.75)
    return series > q3 + factor * (q3 - q1)

sunspot_anom = iqr_anomalies(df["Sunspot Number"].dropna())
kp_anom = iqr_anomalies(df["Estimated K Max"].dropna())

# Combine: anomalous if EITHER indicator is extreme
iqr_mask = pd.Series(False, index=df.index)
iqr_mask.loc[sunspot_anom.index] = iqr_mask.loc[sunspot_anom.index] | sunspot_anom
iqr_mask.loc[kp_anom.index] = iqr_mask.loc[kp_anom.index] | kp_anom
df["iqr_anomaly"] = iqr_mask

print(f"IQR method results:")
print(f"  Sunspot Number anomalies: {sunspot_anom.sum():,}")
print(f"  Estimated Kp max anomalies: {kp_anom.sum():,}")
print(f"  Combined (either): {iqr_mask.sum():,} days ({100*iqr_mask.mean():.1f}% of dataset)")
IQR method results:
  Sunspot Number anomalies: 114
  Estimated Kp max anomalies: 37
  Combined (either): 147 days (1.6% of dataset)

5.2 Isolation Forest (Machine Learning)

Code 
# Isolation Forest anomaly detection
feature_cols = [
    "Sunspot Number", "Radio Flux 10.7cm",
    "Flares: C", "Flares: M", "Flares: X",
    "Estimated K Max", "Estimated A"
]

# Drop rows with NaN in any feature
df_ml = df[["Date"] + feature_cols].dropna().copy()
X = df_ml[feature_cols].values

# Fit Isolation Forest (expect ~2% extreme events)
iso_forest = IsolationForest(contamination=0.02, random_state=42, n_estimators=200)
iso_forest.fit(X)

df_ml["iso_anomaly"] = iso_forest.predict(X) == -1
df["iso_anomaly"] = False
df.loc[df_ml.index, "iso_anomaly"] = df_ml["iso_anomaly"].values

print(f"Isolation Forest results:")
print(f"  Anomalies detected: {df_ml['iso_anomaly'].sum():,} days")
print(f"  ({100 * df_ml['iso_anomaly'].mean():.1f}% of clean feature rows)")
Isolation Forest results:
  Anomalies detected: 186 days
  (2.0% of clean feature rows)

NoteSupervised vs. Unsupervised Anomaly Detection

Both methods used here are unsupervised, they don’t require labelled examples of “extreme events.”

  • IQR method: Purely statistical; assumes anomalies are values far from the central distribution. Simple and interpretable, but considers only one variable at a time.
  • Isolation Forest: A tree-based algorithm that isolates observations by randomly selecting features and split values. Anomalies, being rare and different, require fewer splits to isolate. It naturally handles multivariate interactions.

A supervised approach (training a classifier on confirmed storm catalogues) could be more precise but requires curated labels, which are difficult to obtain for the full range of space weather phenomena.

6. Time-Series Forecasting: Predicting Solar Activity

Can we predict solar activity? The ~11-year solar cycle provides a strong periodic signal, but the amplitude and timing of each cycle are notoriously difficult to forecast. Let’s test two approaches on monthly-averaged sunspot numbers: a classical SARIMA model and Facebook’s Prophet.

6.1 Stationarity Analysis

Code 
# Resample to monthly means
monthly = df.set_index("Date").resample("ME").mean(numeric_only=True).reset_index()
monthly = monthly.dropna(subset=["Sunspot Number"])

print(f"Monthly series: {len(monthly)} observations "
      f"({monthly['Date'].min().strftime('%Y-%m')} to {monthly['Date'].max().strftime('%Y-%m')})\n")

# ADF test on raw monthly sunspot number
result = adfuller(monthly["Sunspot Number"].dropna(), autolag="AIC")
print("Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test (raw series):")
print(f"  Test statistic: {result[0]:.4f}")
print(f"  p-value:        {result[1]:.4f}")
print(f"  Lags used:      {result[2]}")
for key, val in result[4].items():
    print(f"  Critical value ({key}): {val:.4f}")

if result[1] < 0.05:
    print("\n=> Series is STATIONARY (p < 0.05).")
else:
    print("\n=> Series is NON-STATIONARY (p >= 0.05). Differencing required.")
    diff1 = monthly["Sunspot Number"].diff().dropna()
    result_d = adfuller(diff1, autolag="AIC")
    print(f"\nADF on first-differenced series:")
    print(f"  Test statistic: {result_d[0]:.4f}")
    print(f"  p-value:        {result_d[1]:.4f}")
    if result_d[1] < 0.05:
        print("  => First difference is stationary.")

6.2 SARIMA Model

Code 
# Train/test split
train = monthly[monthly["Date"] < "2022-01-01"].copy()
test = monthly[monthly["Date"] >= "2022-01-01"].copy()

print(f"Training: {len(train)} months ({train['Date'].min().strftime('%Y-%m')} to {train['Date'].max().strftime('%Y-%m')})")
print(f"Testing:  {len(test)} months ({test['Date'].min().strftime('%Y-%m')} to {test['Date'].max().strftime('%Y-%m')})")

# Fit SARIMA
try:
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        sarima_model = SARIMAX(
            train["Sunspot Number"],
            order=(1, 1, 1),
            seasonal_order=(1, 1, 1, 12),
            enforce_stationarity=False,
            enforce_invertibility=False,
        )
        sarima_result = sarima_model.fit(disp=False, maxiter=500)

    print(f"\nSARIMA(1,1,1)(1,1,1,12) fitted successfully.")
    print(f"  AIC: {sarima_result.aic:.1f}")
    print(f"  BIC: {sarima_result.bic:.1f}")

    sarima_forecast = sarima_result.get_forecast(steps=len(test))
    sarima_pred = np.maximum(sarima_forecast.predicted_mean.values, 0)
    sarima_ci = sarima_forecast.conf_int()

    sarima_mae = np.mean(np.abs(test["Sunspot Number"].values - sarima_pred))
    sarima_rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((test["Sunspot Number"].values - sarima_pred) ** 2))
    print(f"\n  MAE:  {sarima_mae:.2f}")
    print(f"  RMSE: {sarima_rmse:.2f}")
    sarima_success = True
except Exception as e:
    print(f"SARIMA fitting failed: {e}")
    sarima_success = False

6.3 Prophet Model

Code 
# Prepare data in Prophet format
prophet_train = train[["Date", "Sunspot Number"]].rename(columns={"Date": "ds", "Sunspot Number": "y"})

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    prophet_model = Prophet(
        yearly_seasonality=True, weekly_seasonality=False,
        daily_seasonality=False, changepoint_prior_scale=0.05,
    )
    prophet_model.fit(prophet_train)

future = prophet_model.make_future_dataframe(periods=len(test), freq="ME")
prophet_forecast = prophet_model.predict(future)

prophet_test_pred = prophet_forecast.tail(len(test))
prophet_pred = np.maximum(prophet_test_pred["yhat"].values, 0)
prophet_lower = np.maximum(prophet_test_pred["yhat_lower"].values, 0)
prophet_upper = prophet_test_pred["yhat_upper"].values

prophet_mae = np.mean(np.abs(test["Sunspot Number"].values - prophet_pred))
prophet_rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((test["Sunspot Number"].values - prophet_pred) ** 2))

print(f"Prophet model fitted successfully.")
print(f"  MAE:  {prophet_mae:.2f}")
print(f"  RMSE: {prophet_rmse:.2f}")
prophet_success = True
Prophet model fitted successfully.

TipWhy Solar Cycle Prediction is Hard

The solar dynamo is a chaotic, nonlinear system. While the ~11-year periodicity is robust, the amplitude of each cycle varies dramatically. Key challenges:

  1. No perfect periodicity: Cycle lengths range from 9 to 14 years, making seasonal modelling imprecise.
  2. Amplitude unpredictability: Physical models of the solar dynamo still struggle to predict the strength of the next cycle years in advance.
  3. Stochastic bursts: Individual flares and CMEs are essentially unpredictable more than a few days out.

State-of-the-art predictions combine statistical models with physics-based solar dynamo simulations and precursor methods (using polar magnetic field measurements to predict the next cycle’s strength).

# Panel 4: Radio Flux
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scattergl(
    x=df_sorted["Date"], y=df_sorted["Radio Flux 10.7cm"],
    mode="markers", marker=dict(size=1.5, color=SOLAR_SECONDARY, opacity=0.2),
    name="Daily F10.7", showlegend=False,
), row=2, col=2)
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=df_sorted["Date"], y=df_sorted["F107_MA30"],
    mode="lines", line=dict(color=SOLAR_SECONDARY, width=2),
    name="F10.7 (30d MA)",
), row=2, col=2)

# Synchronize x-axes and add range slider
fig_dash.update_xaxes(matches="x")
fig_dash.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True, row=2, col=2)

fig_dash.update_yaxes(title_text="Sunspot Number", row=1, col=1)
fig_dash.update_yaxes(title_text="Kp (max)", row=1, col=2)
fig_dash.update_yaxes(title_text="Flares / day (30d avg)", row=2, col=1)
fig_dash.update_yaxes(title_text="SFU", row=2, col=2)

fig_dash.update_layout(
    title="Space Weather Dashboard: Solar & Geomagnetic Activity (1997-2024)",
    height=800,
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.15, xanchor="center", x=0.5, font=dict(size=10)),
    margin=dict(b=120),
)
fig_dash.show()

Key Takeaways

  • The ~11-year solar cycle is the dominant rhythm in nearly every variable, sunspot numbers, radio flux, and flare rates all rise and fall in concert, though individual cycles differ substantially in amplitude.
  • Geomagnetic activity lags solar activity by 1–2 days for flare-associated CME events, as confirmed by our superposed epoch analysis.
  • X-class flares are rare but impactful, they make up a tiny fraction of all flares yet produce the most severe geomagnetic storms.
  • Forecasting solar activity remains challenging: While the periodic component is captured by SARIMA and Prophet, the chaotic nature of the solar dynamo limits predictability.
  • Multi-instrument monitoring is essential, no single index tells the whole story. The dashboard above shows how combining sunspot counts, radio flux, flare rates, and geomagnetic indices gives a far richer picture.
NoteFurther Resources
  • NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center: swpc.noaa.gov, real-time forecasts, alerts, and educational material
  • Kaggle Dataset: Space Weather, Solar & Geomagnetic Indices
  • NASA DONKI: kauai.ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI, Database for tracking CMEs, flares, and storms

## 1. When the Sun Throws a Tantrum

On October 28, 2003, the Sun threw a tantrum so violent it rewrote the textbooks. A colossal X17.2 flare --- one of the most powerful ever recorded --- erupted from sunspot region 486, hurling a wall of magnetized plasma toward Earth at over 2,000 km/s. Within hours, airline flights were rerouted over the poles, satellites tumbled out of orientation, and the Swedish power grid went dark. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station retreated to shielded modules. Auroras --- normally confined to the Arctic --- painted the skies as far south as Florida and Texas.

That week, known as the **Halloween Solar Storms**, was not an anomaly. It was a reminder: our star is not the calm, steady lantern it appears to be. It breathes, it cycles, it rages --- and our increasingly electrified civilization sits squarely in the blast zone.

This notebook explores **27 years of space weather data** (1997--2024), spanning nearly three complete solar cycles. We will trace the Sun's heartbeat through sunspot counts and radio flux, decode the geomagnetic tremors it sends rippling through Earth's magnetosphere, and hunt for the patterns that connect solar fury to terrestrial disruption.

::: {.callout-note}
## What is Space Weather?

**Space weather** describes the conditions in the space environment between the Sun and Earth. It is driven by the Sun's magnetic activity and affects:

- **Satellite operations** --- charged particles degrade solar panels and corrupt electronics
- **GPS and communications** --- ionospheric disturbances cause positioning errors and radio blackouts
- **Power grids** --- geomagnetically induced currents can overload transformers (the 1989 Quebec blackout left 6 million people without power for 9 hours)
- **Astronaut safety** --- solar energetic particles pose a serious radiation hazard
- **Aviation** --- high-latitude flights receive increased radiation doses during solar storms

Understanding space weather is not just academic curiosity --- it is critical infrastructure protection.
:::

### Loading and Cleaning the Data

```{python}
# Download dataset from Kaggle
path = kagglehub.dataset_download("erevear/space-weather-solar-geomagnetic-indices")

# Load both CSV files
solar_raw = pd.read_csv(f"{path}/daily_solar_data.csv")
geo_raw = pd.read_csv(f"{path}/daily_geomagnetic_data.csv")

print(f"Solar data (raw):        {solar_raw.shape[0]:,} rows x {solar_raw.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"Geomagnetic data (raw):  {geo_raw.shape[0]:,} rows x {geo_raw.shape[1]} columns")
```

```{python}
# --- Solar data cleaning ---
solar = solar_raw.copy()

# Drop duplicate dates (457 duplicates from 2017-2018)
solar = solar.drop_duplicates(subset="Date", keep="first").reset_index(drop=True)

# Parse dates
solar["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(solar["Date"])

# Replace sentinels with NaN
for col in solar.columns:
    if solar[col].dtype == object and col != "Date":
        solar[col] = solar[col].replace("*", np.nan)
        solar[col] = pd.to_numeric(solar[col], errors="coerce")

# -999 sentinel in Stanford fields, -1 in flare columns
stanford_cols = [c for c in solar.columns if "Stanford" in c]
solar[stanford_cols] = solar[stanford_cols].replace(-999, np.nan)

flare_cols = [c for c in solar.columns if "Flares" in c]
solar[flare_cols] = solar[flare_cols].replace(-1, np.nan)

# Ensure all numeric columns are proper numeric types
for col in [c for c in solar.columns if c != "Date"]:
    solar[col] = pd.to_numeric(solar[col], errors="coerce")

# --- Geomagnetic data cleaning ---
geo = geo_raw.copy()

# Drop duplicate timestamps (7264 duplicates)
geo = geo.drop_duplicates(subset="Timestamp", keep="first").reset_index(drop=True)

# Parse timestamps and replace sentinels
geo["Timestamp"] = pd.to_datetime(geo["Timestamp"])

for col in geo.columns:
    if geo[col].dtype == object and col != "Timestamp":
        geo[col] = geo[col].replace("*", np.nan)
        geo[col] = pd.to_numeric(geo[col], errors="coerce")

for col in [c for c in geo.columns if c != "Timestamp"]:
    geo[col] = pd.to_numeric(geo[col], errors="coerce")
    geo[col] = geo[col].replace(-1, np.nan)

# Create date column for daily aggregation
geo["Date"] = geo["Timestamp"].dt.normalize()

# A-indices: daily (repeated 8x) -> take first
# K-indices: true 3-hourly -> compute mean and max per day
a_cols = ["Middle Latitude A", "High Latitude A", "Estimated A"]
k_cols = ["Middle Latitude K", "High Latitude K", "Estimated K"]

geo_a = geo.groupby("Date")[a_cols].first().reset_index()
geo_k_mean = geo.groupby("Date")[k_cols].mean().reset_index()
geo_k_mean.columns = ["Date"] + [f"{c} Mean" for c in k_cols]
geo_k_max = geo.groupby("Date")[k_cols].max().reset_index()
geo_k_max.columns = ["Date"] + [f"{c} Max" for c in k_cols]

geo_daily = geo_a.merge(geo_k_mean, on="Date").merge(geo_k_max, on="Date")

# --- Merge solar + geomagnetic on Date ---
df = solar.merge(geo_daily, on="Date", how="inner")
df = df.sort_values("Date").reset_index(drop=True)

print(f"\nAfter cleaning:")
print(f"  Solar:        {solar.shape[0]:,} rows x {solar.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"  Geomagnetic:  {geo_daily.shape[0]:,} rows x {geo_daily.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"  Merged:       {df.shape[0]:,} rows x {df.shape[1]} columns")
print(f"  Date range:   {df['Date'].min().strftime('%Y-%m-%d')} to {df['Date'].max().strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key Space Weather Indices

The dataset tracks several complementary measures of solar and geomagnetic activity:

**Solar indices:**

- **Sunspot Number (SSN)** --- a count of dark, magnetically active spots on the Sun's visible disk. More sunspots = more active Sun. The primary tracker of the ~11-year solar cycle.
- **F10.7 Radio Flux** --- solar radio emission at 10.7 cm wavelength (2800 MHz), measured in Solar Flux Units (SFU). Correlates tightly with sunspot number but can be measured through clouds and at night.
- **Solar Flares (C / M / X)** --- sudden bursts of electromagnetic radiation, classified on a logarithmic scale: C-class (minor), M-class (moderate, 10x C), X-class (extreme, 10x M). An X10 flare is 1,000x more powerful than a C1.

**Geomagnetic indices:**

- **K-index (Kp)** --- a quasi-logarithmic 0--9 scale measuring geomagnetic disturbance over 3-hour intervals. K >= 5 indicates a geomagnetic storm.
- **A-index (Ap)** --- a daily linearized equivalent of the K-index. Ap >= 50 signals a significant storm; Ap >= 100 is severe.
:::

## 2. The Solar Heartbeat: 11-Year Cycles

The Sun is not a static ball of fire --- it is a churning, magnetized dynamo with a pulse. Roughly every **11 years**, the Sun's magnetic field undergoes a dramatic reversal: its north and south magnetic poles flip. This magnetic cycle drives the rise and fall of sunspot activity, flare frequency, and coronal mass ejections.

Our dataset spans the tail end of **Solar Cycle 23** (which peaked around 2000--2002), the entirety of the unusually weak **Cycle 24** (peak ~2014), and the ascending phase of **Cycle 25** (currently underway, with activity ramping up sharply since 2022).


::: {.callout-note}
## Why 11 Years?

The solar cycle is driven by the Sun's **differential rotation** --- the equator rotates faster than the poles. This shearing motion stretches and tangles the Sun's magnetic field lines over time, building up magnetic stress. Sunspots emerge where tangled magnetic flux tubes break through the surface.

After roughly 11 years, the accumulated tangling causes the global magnetic field to **reverse polarity** (north becomes south). The full magnetic cycle is actually **22 years** --- it takes two reversals to return to the original configuration --- but the 11-year activity cycle is what we observe most directly.

Cycle 24 (2008--2019) was notably weaker than its predecessors, leading some solar physicists to speculate about a possible grand minimum. Cycle 25, however, has exceeded all predictions and is shaping up to be significantly stronger than Cycle 24.
:::

```{python}
# Assign solar cycle labels
def assign_cycle(date):
    if date < pd.Timestamp("2008-12-01"):
        return "Cycle 23"
    elif date < pd.Timestamp("2019-12-01"):
        return "Cycle 24"
    else:
        return "Cycle 25"

df["Solar Cycle"] = df["Date"].apply(assign_cycle)

# Yearly average sunspot number
yearly = df.groupby([df["Date"].dt.year, "Solar Cycle"]).agg(
    SSN_mean=("Sunspot Number", "mean")
).reset_index()
yearly.columns = ["Year", "Solar Cycle", "SSN_mean"]

cycle_colors = {"Cycle 23": SOLAR_PRIMARY, "Cycle 24": SOLAR_SECONDARY, "Cycle 25": ALERT_COLOR}

fig_yearly = go.Figure()
for cycle in ["Cycle 23", "Cycle 24", "Cycle 25"]:
    mask = yearly["Solar Cycle"] == cycle
    fig_yearly.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=yearly.loc[mask, "Year"], y=yearly.loc[mask, "SSN_mean"],
        name=cycle, marker_color=cycle_colors[cycle],
        hovertemplate="Year: %{x}<br>Mean SSN: %{y:.1f}<extra>" + cycle + "</extra>",
    ))

fig_yearly.update_layout(
    title="Yearly Average Sunspot Number by Solar Cycle",
    xaxis_title="Year", yaxis_title="Mean Daily Sunspot Number",
    height=420, margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=50, b=40),
    barmode="stack",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.2, xanchor="center", x=0.5),
    yaxis_rangemode="tozero",
)
fig_yearly.show()
```

The cyclic pattern is unmistakable. Each cycle rises over ~4 years, peaks, then declines over ~7 years. Notice how Cycle 24's peak (annual mean SSN around 80--110) was roughly half the amplitude of Cycle 23 --- and how Cycle 25 has already surpassed Cycle 24's maximum, defying the conservative forecasts issued at its onset.

## 3. The Sun-Earth Connection: Multi-Variable Correlation

Solar activity does not happen in isolation. A burst of X-ray flares on the Sun's surface can trigger a cascade that reaches Earth within minutes (electromagnetic radiation) to days (coronal mass ejections). But how tightly are these phenomena coupled in the data?

```{python}
# Correlation heatmap
corr_cols = [
    "Sunspot Number", "Radio Flux 10.7cm", "Sunspot Area (10^6 Hemis.)",
    "Flares: C", "Flares: M", "Flares: X",
    "Estimated A", "Estimated K Mean",
]
corr_labels = ["Sunspot Number", "F10.7 Flux", "Sunspot Area",
               "Flares C", "Flares M", "Flares X", "A-index", "K Mean"]

corr_matrix = df[corr_cols].corr(method="pearson")

space_colorscale = [
    [0.0, GEO_PRIMARY], [0.25, "#a8d8f0"],
    [0.5, "#f5f5f5"], [0.75, "#ffb899"], [1.0, SOLAR_PRIMARY],
]

z_text = [[f"{val:.2f}" for val in row] for row in corr_matrix.values]

fig_corr = go.Figure(data=go.Heatmap(
    z=corr_matrix.values, x=corr_labels, y=corr_labels,
    colorscale=space_colorscale, zmin=-1, zmax=1,
    text=z_text, texttemplate="%{text}", textfont=dict(size=11),
    hovertemplate="(%{x}, %{y})<br>r = %{z:.3f}<extra></extra>",
    colorbar=dict(title="Pearson r", thickness=15, len=0.8),
))

fig_corr.update_layout(
    title="Correlation Matrix, Solar & Geomagnetic Indices",
    height=550, width=680,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=50, b=20),
    xaxis=dict(tickangle=-40, side="bottom"),
    yaxis=dict(autorange="reversed"),
)
fig_corr.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Correlation Is Not Causation --- But Here, the Physics Is Clear

In most datasets, we caution against interpreting correlation as causation. Space weather is one of the rare domains where the **causal chain is unambiguous and well-understood**:

1. **Magnetic dynamo** in the Sun's interior generates sunspots and active regions
2. **Active regions** produce solar flares (C, M, X-class) and coronal mass ejections (CMEs)
3. **Flares** emit X-rays and UV radiation that disturb Earth's ionosphere within 8 minutes
4. **CMEs** launch magnetized plasma that impacts Earth's magnetosphere 1--3 days later
5. **Magnetospheric compression** drives geomagnetic storms measured by K and A indices
:::

```{python}
# Scatter matrix: 3 key relationships
fig_scatter = make_subplots(
    rows=1, cols=3,
    subplot_titles=["SSN vs F10.7 Radio Flux", "X-class Flares vs K Mean", "SSN vs A-index"],
    horizontal_spacing=0.08,
)

# Panel 1: SSN vs Radio Flux
mask1 = df[["Sunspot Number", "Radio Flux 10.7cm"]].notna().all(axis=1)
x1, y1 = df.loc[mask1, "Sunspot Number"], df.loc[mask1, "Radio Flux 10.7cm"]
fig_scatter.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x1, y=y1, mode="markers",
    marker=dict(color=SOLAR_PRIMARY, size=3, opacity=0.3),
    name="SSN vs F10.7", showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=1)
slope1, intercept1, r1, _, _ = stats.linregress(x1, y1)
x1_range = np.linspace(x1.min(), x1.max(), 100)
fig_scatter.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x1_range, y=slope1 * x1_range + intercept1,
    mode="lines", line=dict(color=ALERT_COLOR, width=2, dash="dash"),
    name=f"r = {r1:.3f}",
), row=1, col=1)

# Panel 2: Flares X vs K Mean
mask2 = df[["Flares: X", "Estimated K Mean"]].notna().all(axis=1)
x2, y2 = df.loc[mask2, "Flares: X"], df.loc[mask2, "Estimated K Mean"]
fig_scatter.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x2, y=y2, mode="markers",
    marker=dict(color=ALERT_COLOR, size=3, opacity=0.3),
    name="Flares X vs K", showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=2)
slope2, intercept2, r2, _, _ = stats.linregress(x2, y2)
x2_range = np.linspace(x2.min(), x2.max(), 100)
fig_scatter.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x2_range, y=slope2 * x2_range + intercept2,
    mode="lines", line=dict(color=GEO_PRIMARY, width=2, dash="dash"),
    name=f"r = {r2:.3f}",
), row=1, col=2)

# Panel 3: SSN vs A-index
mask3 = df[["Sunspot Number", "Estimated A"]].notna().all(axis=1)
x3, y3 = df.loc[mask3, "Sunspot Number"], df.loc[mask3, "Estimated A"]
fig_scatter.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x3, y=y3, mode="markers",
    marker=dict(color=GEO_PRIMARY, size=3, opacity=0.3),
    name="SSN vs A-index", showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=3)
slope3, intercept3, r3, _, _ = stats.linregress(x3, y3)
x3_range = np.linspace(x3.min(), x3.max(), 100)
fig_scatter.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x3_range, y=slope3 * x3_range + intercept3,
    mode="lines", line=dict(color=SOLAR_SECONDARY, width=2, dash="dash"),
    name=f"r = {r3:.3f}",
), row=1, col=3)

fig_scatter.update_xaxes(title_text="Sunspot Number", row=1, col=1)
fig_scatter.update_yaxes(title_text="F10.7 Flux (SFU)", row=1, col=1)
fig_scatter.update_xaxes(title_text="X-class Flares (daily)", row=1, col=2)
fig_scatter.update_yaxes(title_text="K Mean (daily)", row=1, col=2)
fig_scatter.update_xaxes(title_text="Sunspot Number", row=1, col=3)
fig_scatter.update_yaxes(title_text="A-index", row=1, col=3)

fig_scatter.update_layout(
    title="Key Scatter Relationships, Solar Activity vs Geomagnetic Response",
    height=420, margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=80, b=40),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.25, xanchor="center", x=0.5, font_size=11),
)
fig_scatter.show()
```

Three stories emerge:

- **SSN vs F10.7 Flux** shows a remarkably tight linear relationship --- these two indices are nearly interchangeable proxies for solar activity.
- **X-class Flares vs K Mean** reveals a weaker but meaningful link between extreme solar events and geomagnetic disturbance. The scatter is wide because not every flare produces an Earth-directed CME.
- **SSN vs A-index** shows a positive but diffuse relationship, mediated by the solar wind --- a complex, turbulent intermediary.

## 4. Solar Flares and Geomagnetic Impact

Solar flares are classified on a logarithmic scale based on their peak X-ray flux in the 1--8 Angstrom band. Each class represents a tenfold increase in energy:

| Class | Peak Flux (W/m^2^) | Typical Effects |
|-------|---------------------|-----------------|
| **C** | 10^-6^ -- 10^-5^ | Minor; few noticeable consequences |
| **M** | 10^-5^ -- 10^-4^ | Moderate; brief radio blackouts at poles |
| **X** | > 10^-4^ | Major; wide-area radio blackouts, radiation storms |

When a flare is accompanied by a **Coronal Mass Ejection (CME)**, the ejected plasma compresses our magnetosphere, producing geomagnetic storms. The critical question: *how long after a flare do we see the geomagnetic response?*

```{python}
# Stacked bar chart of flares per year
df["Year"] = df["Date"].dt.year
flares_yearly = df.groupby("Year")[["Flares: C", "Flares: M", "Flares: X"]].sum().reset_index()

fig_flares = go.Figure()
fig_flares.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=flares_yearly["Year"], y=flares_yearly["Flares: C"],
    name="C-class", marker_color=SOLAR_SECONDARY))
fig_flares.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=flares_yearly["Year"], y=flares_yearly["Flares: M"],
    name="M-class", marker_color=SOLAR_PRIMARY))
fig_flares.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=flares_yearly["Year"], y=flares_yearly["Flares: X"],
    name="X-class", marker_color=ALERT_COLOR))

fig_flares.update_layout(
    barmode="stack",
    title="Annual Solar Flare Counts by Classification",
    xaxis_title="Year", yaxis_title="Number of Flares",
    height=500,
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1),
)
fig_flares.show()
```

### The Sun-to-Earth Delay

When an X-class flare erupts, how quickly does Earth feel the geomagnetic effects? Let's measure this delay empirically with a **superposed epoch analysis** --- averaging Kp around all X-flare days.

```{python}
# Superposed epoch analysis: Kp around X-flare days
x_flare_days = df.loc[df["Flares: X"] > 0, "Date"].values

window = range(-3, 4)
epoch_data = {day_offset: [] for day_offset in window}

for flare_date in x_flare_days:
    for offset in window:
        target_date = flare_date + np.timedelta64(offset, "D")
        match = df.loc[df["Date"] == target_date, "Estimated K Max"]
        if len(match) == 1 and not np.isnan(match.values[0]):
            epoch_data[offset].append(match.values[0])

offsets = list(window)
means = [np.mean(epoch_data[o]) if epoch_data[o] else np.nan for o in offsets]
stderrs = [np.std(epoch_data[o]) / np.sqrt(len(epoch_data[o])) if len(epoch_data[o]) > 1 else 0 for o in offsets]

upper = [m + 1.96 * s for m, s in zip(means, stderrs)]
lower = [m - 1.96 * s for m, s in zip(means, stderrs)]

fig_epoch = go.Figure()

# Confidence band
fig_epoch.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=offsets + offsets[::-1], y=upper + lower[::-1],
    fill="toself", fillcolor="rgba(239,71,111,0.15)",
    line=dict(color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"), showlegend=False, name="95% CI",
))

# Mean line
fig_epoch.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=offsets, y=means, mode="lines+markers",
    line=dict(color=ALERT_COLOR, width=3),
    marker=dict(size=10, color=ALERT_COLOR), name="Mean Kp (max)",
))

fig_epoch.add_shape(
    type="line", x0=0, x1=0, y0=0, y1=1, yref="paper",
    line=dict(color=NEUTRAL, width=1.5, dash="dash"),
)
fig_epoch.add_annotation(
    x=0, y=1.05, yref="paper", text="Flare day",
    showarrow=False, font=dict(size=11, color=NEUTRAL),
)

fig_epoch.update_layout(
    title="Superposed Epoch Analysis: Kp Response to X-class Flares",
    xaxis_title="Days Relative to X-class Flare",
    yaxis_title="Average Estimated Kp (max)",
    height=450,
)
fig_epoch.show()
```

The superposed epoch analysis reveals the expected pattern: Kp tends to peak **1--2 days after** an X-class flare, consistent with CME transit times.

```{python}
# Violin plot: Kp distribution by flare activity level
def classify_flare_day(row):
    if row["Flares: X"] > 0:
        return "X-class"
    elif row["Flares: M"] > 0:
        return "M-class"
    elif row["Flares: C"] > 0:
        return "C-only"
    else:

df["flare_category"] = df.apply(classify_flare_day, axis=1)

cat_order = ["Quiet", "C-only", "M-class", "X-class"]
cat_colors = {"Quiet": NEUTRAL, "C-only": SOLAR_SECONDARY, "M-class": SOLAR_PRIMARY, "X-class": ALERT_COLOR}

fig_violin = go.Figure()
for cat in cat_order:
    subset = df.loc[df["flare_category"] == cat, "Estimated K Max"].dropna()
    if len(subset) < 2:
        continue
    fig_violin.add_trace(go.Violin(
        y=subset, name=cat, box_visible=True, meanline_visible=True,

    ))

fig_violin.update_layout(
```

The violin plots show a clear upward shift: days with M-class and X-class flares tend to have higher Kp values, though the overlap is substantial --- not every powerful flare produces a geomagnetic storm.

::: {.callout-tip}
## CME Travel Time

A Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) is a massive expulsion of magnetised plasma from the solar corona. Typical CME speeds range from **400 to 2000+ km/s**. At these speeds, the Sun-Earth distance of ~150 million km is covered in:

- **Slow CME (~400 km/s):** ~4 days
- **Average CME (~800 km/s):** ~2 days
- **Fast CME (~2000 km/s):** ~18 hours

This is why we observe a **1--3 day lag** between a solar flare and the onset of a geomagnetic storm.
:::

## 5. Anomaly Detection: Finding Extreme Space Weather

Extreme space weather events are rare but consequential. The Carrington Event of 1859 remains the most powerful recorded geomagnetic storm --- if it happened today, it could cause trillions of dollars in damage. Can we systematically detect anomalous days in our dataset?

We compare two approaches: a **classical statistical method** (IQR) and a **machine learning method** (Isolation Forest).

### 5.1 IQR Method (Statistical Baseline)

```{python}
# IQR-based anomaly detection
def iqr_anomalies(series, factor=1.5):
    """Flag values above Q3 + factor * IQR as anomalies."""
    q1, q3 = series.quantile(0.25), series.quantile(0.75)
    return series > q3 + factor * (q3 - q1)

sunspot_anom = iqr_anomalies(df["Sunspot Number"].dropna())
kp_anom = iqr_anomalies(df["Estimated K Max"].dropna())

# Combine: anomalous if EITHER indicator is extreme
iqr_mask = pd.Series(False, index=df.index)
iqr_mask.loc[sunspot_anom.index] = iqr_mask.loc[sunspot_anom.index] | sunspot_anom
iqr_mask.loc[kp_anom.index] = iqr_mask.loc[kp_anom.index] | kp_anom
df["iqr_anomaly"] = iqr_mask

print(f"IQR method results:")
print(f"  Sunspot Number anomalies: {sunspot_anom.sum():,}")
print(f"  Estimated Kp max anomalies: {kp_anom.sum():,}")
print(f"  Combined (either): {iqr_mask.sum():,} days ({100*iqr_mask.mean():.1f}% of dataset)")
```

### 5.2 Isolation Forest (Machine Learning)

```{python}
# Isolation Forest anomaly detection
feature_cols = [
    "Sunspot Number", "Radio Flux 10.7cm",
    "Flares: C", "Flares: M", "Flares: X",
    "Estimated K Max", "Estimated A"
]

# Drop rows with NaN in any feature
df_ml = df[["Date"] + feature_cols].dropna().copy()
X = df_ml[feature_cols].values

# Fit Isolation Forest (expect ~2% extreme events)
iso_forest = IsolationForest(contamination=0.02, random_state=42, n_estimators=200)
iso_forest.fit(X)

df_ml["iso_anomaly"] = iso_forest.predict(X) == -1
df["iso_anomaly"] = False
df.loc[df_ml.index, "iso_anomaly"] = df_ml["iso_anomaly"].values

print(f"Isolation Forest results:")
print(f"  Anomalies detected: {df_ml['iso_anomaly'].sum():,} days")
print(f"  ({100 * df_ml['iso_anomaly'].mean():.1f}% of clean feature rows)")
```

### 5.3 Comparison: Where Do the Methods Agree?

```{python}
# Classify each day by detection method
def detection_label(row):
    iqr = row.get("iqr_anomaly", False)
    iso = row.get("iso_anomaly", False)
    if iqr and iso:
        return "Both methods"
    elif iqr:
        return "IQR only"
    elif iso:
        return "Isolation Forest only"
    else:
        return "Normal"

df["detection"] = df.apply(detection_label, axis=1)

det_colors = {
    "Normal": NEUTRAL, "IQR only": SOLAR_SECONDARY,
    "Isolation Forest only": GEO_PRIMARY, "Both methods": ALERT_COLOR,
}

fig_anom = go.Figure()
for label in ["Normal", "IQR only", "Isolation Forest only", "Both methods"]:
    subset = df[df["detection"] == label]
    fig_anom.add_trace(go.Scattergl(
        x=subset["Date"], y=subset["Sunspot Number"],
        mode="markers",
        marker=dict(
            size=3 if label == "Normal" else 6,
            color=det_colors[label],
            opacity=0.3 if label == "Normal" else 0.8,
        ),
        name=label,
    ))

# Annotate known extreme events
known_events = [
    ("2000-07-14", "Bastille Day\nEvent"),
    ("2003-10-28", "Halloween\nStorms"),
    ("2015-03-17", "St. Patrick's\nDay Storm"),
]
for date_str, event_name in known_events:
    event_date = pd.Timestamp(date_str)
    match = df.loc[df["Date"] == event_date]
    if len(match) > 0:
        fig_anom.add_annotation(
            x=event_date, y=match["Sunspot Number"].values[0],
            text=event_name, showarrow=True, arrowhead=2,
            arrowcolor=ALERT_COLOR, font=dict(size=10, color=ALERT_COLOR),
            ax=0, ay=-50,
        )

fig_anom.update_layout(
    title="Anomaly Detection: IQR vs Isolation Forest (Sunspot Number)",
    xaxis_title="Date", yaxis_title="Sunspot Number",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1),
    height=550,
)
fig_anom.show()
```

### 5.4 Top Anomalous Days

```{python}
# Top 10 most anomalous days (scored by Isolation Forest)
df_scored = df_ml.copy()
df_scored["anomaly_score"] = iso_forest.decision_function(X)

top10 = df_scored.nsmallest(10, "anomaly_score")[
    ["Date", "Sunspot Number", "Radio Flux 10.7cm",
     "Flares: M", "Flares: X", "Estimated K Max", "Estimated A", "anomaly_score"]
].copy()

top10["Date"] = top10["Date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
top10["anomaly_score"] = top10["anomaly_score"].round(4)
top10.columns = ["Date", "Sunspots", "F10.7", "M-flares", "X-flares", "Kp max", "Ap", "Anomaly Score"]

print("Top 10 Most Anomalous Days (lowest Isolation Forest score = most anomalous):\n")
print(top10.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Supervised vs. Unsupervised Anomaly Detection

Both methods used here are **unsupervised** --- they don't require labelled examples of "extreme events."

- **IQR method**: Purely statistical; assumes anomalies are values far from the central distribution. Simple and interpretable, but considers only one variable at a time.
- **Isolation Forest**: A tree-based algorithm that isolates observations by randomly selecting features and split values. Anomalies --- being rare and different --- require fewer splits to isolate. It naturally handles multivariate interactions.

A **supervised** approach (training a classifier on confirmed storm catalogues) could be more precise but requires curated labels, which are difficult to obtain for the full range of space weather phenomena.
:::

## 6. Time-Series Forecasting: Predicting Solar Activity

Can we predict solar activity? The ~11-year solar cycle provides a strong periodic signal, but the *amplitude* and *timing* of each cycle are notoriously difficult to forecast. Let's test two approaches on monthly-averaged sunspot numbers: a classical **SARIMA** model and Facebook's **Prophet**.

### 6.1 Stationarity Analysis

```{python}
# Resample to monthly means
monthly = df.set_index("Date").resample("ME").mean(numeric_only=True).reset_index()
monthly = monthly.dropna(subset=["Sunspot Number"])

print(f"Monthly series: {len(monthly)} observations "
      f"({monthly['Date'].min().strftime('%Y-%m')} to {monthly['Date'].max().strftime('%Y-%m')})\n")

# ADF test on raw monthly sunspot number
result = adfuller(monthly["Sunspot Number"].dropna(), autolag="AIC")
print("Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test (raw series):")
print(f"  Test statistic: {result[0]:.4f}")
print(f"  p-value:        {result[1]:.4f}")
print(f"  Lags used:      {result[2]}")
for key, val in result[4].items():
    print(f"  Critical value ({key}): {val:.4f}")

if result[1] < 0.05:
    print("\n=> Series is STATIONARY (p < 0.05).")
else:
    print("\n=> Series is NON-STATIONARY (p >= 0.05). Differencing required.")
    diff1 = monthly["Sunspot Number"].diff().dropna()
    result_d = adfuller(diff1, autolag="AIC")
    print(f"\nADF on first-differenced series:")
    print(f"  Test statistic: {result_d[0]:.4f}")
    print(f"  p-value:        {result_d[1]:.4f}")
    if result_d[1] < 0.05:
        print("  => First difference is stationary.")
```

### 6.2 SARIMA Model

```{python}
# Train/test split
train = monthly[monthly["Date"] < "2022-01-01"].copy()
test = monthly[monthly["Date"] >= "2022-01-01"].copy()

print(f"Training: {len(train)} months ({train['Date'].min().strftime('%Y-%m')} to {train['Date'].max().strftime('%Y-%m')})")
print(f"Testing:  {len(test)} months ({test['Date'].min().strftime('%Y-%m')} to {test['Date'].max().strftime('%Y-%m')})")

# Fit SARIMA
try:
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        sarima_model = SARIMAX(
            train["Sunspot Number"],
            order=(1, 1, 1),
            seasonal_order=(1, 1, 1, 12),
            enforce_stationarity=False,
            enforce_invertibility=False,
        )
        sarima_result = sarima_model.fit(disp=False, maxiter=500)

    print(f"\nSARIMA(1,1,1)(1,1,1,12) fitted successfully.")
    print(f"  AIC: {sarima_result.aic:.1f}")
    print(f"  BIC: {sarima_result.bic:.1f}")

    sarima_forecast = sarima_result.get_forecast(steps=len(test))
    sarima_pred = np.maximum(sarima_forecast.predicted_mean.values, 0)
    sarima_ci = sarima_forecast.conf_int()

    sarima_mae = np.mean(np.abs(test["Sunspot Number"].values - sarima_pred))
    sarima_rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((test["Sunspot Number"].values - sarima_pred) ** 2))
    print(f"\n  MAE:  {sarima_mae:.2f}")
    print(f"  RMSE: {sarima_rmse:.2f}")
    sarima_success = True
except Exception as e:
    print(f"SARIMA fitting failed: {e}")
    sarima_success = False
```

### 6.3 Prophet Model

```{python}
# Prepare data in Prophet format
prophet_train = train[["Date", "Sunspot Number"]].rename(columns={"Date": "ds", "Sunspot Number": "y"})

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    prophet_model = Prophet(
        yearly_seasonality=True, weekly_seasonality=False,
        daily_seasonality=False, changepoint_prior_scale=0.05,
    )
    prophet_model.fit(prophet_train)

future = prophet_model.make_future_dataframe(periods=len(test), freq="ME")
prophet_forecast = prophet_model.predict(future)

prophet_test_pred = prophet_forecast.tail(len(test))
prophet_pred = np.maximum(prophet_test_pred["yhat"].values, 0)
prophet_lower = np.maximum(prophet_test_pred["yhat_lower"].values, 0)
prophet_upper = prophet_test_pred["yhat_upper"].values

prophet_mae = np.mean(np.abs(test["Sunspot Number"].values - prophet_pred))
prophet_rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((test["Sunspot Number"].values - prophet_pred) ** 2))

print(f"Prophet model fitted successfully.")
print(f"  MAE:  {prophet_mae:.2f}")
print(f"  RMSE: {prophet_rmse:.2f}")
prophet_success = True
```

### 6.4 Forecast Comparison

```{python}
fig_forecast = go.Figure()

# Training data (last 5 years for context)
train_tail = train[train["Date"] >= "2017-01-01"]
fig_forecast.add_trace(go.Scatter(

))

# SARIMA forecast + CI
if sarima_success:
    ci_lower = np.maximum(sarima_ci.iloc[:, 0].values, 0)
    ci_upper = sarima_ci.iloc[:, 1].values
    fig_forecast.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=pd.concat([test["Date"], test["Date"].iloc[::-1]]),
        y=np.concatenate([ci_upper, ci_lower[::-1]]),
        fill="toself", fillcolor="rgba(255,107,53,0.12)",
        line=dict(color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"), showlegend=False, name="SARIMA CI",
    ))
    fig_forecast.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=test["Date"], y=sarima_pred,
        mode="lines", name=f"SARIMA (MAE={sarima_mae:.1f})",
        line=dict(color=SOLAR_PRIMARY, width=2, dash="dash"),
    ))

# Prophet forecast + CI
if prophet_success:
    fig_forecast.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=pd.concat([test["Date"], test["Date"].iloc[::-1]]),
        y=np.concatenate([prophet_upper, prophet_lower[::-1]]),
        fill="toself", fillcolor="rgba(27,152,224,0.12)",
        line=dict(color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"), showlegend=False, name="Prophet CI",
    ))
    fig_forecast.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=test["Date"], y=prophet_pred,
        mode="lines", name=f"Prophet (MAE={prophet_mae:.1f})",
        line=dict(color=GEO_PRIMARY, width=2, dash="dot"),
    ))

fig_forecast.add_shape(
    type="line", x0="2022-01-01", x1="2022-01-01",
    y0=0, y1=1, yref="paper",
    line=dict(color=NEUTRAL, width=1.5, dash="dash"),
)
fig_forecast.add_annotation(
    x="2022-01-01", y=1.05, yref="paper",
    text="Train / Test split", showarrow=False,
    font=dict(size=11, color=NEUTRAL),
)

fig_forecast.update_layout(
    title="Monthly Sunspot Number: SARIMA vs Prophet Forecasts",
    xaxis_title="Date", yaxis_title="Monthly Mean Sunspot Number",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1),
    height=550,
)
fig_forecast.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why Solar Cycle Prediction is Hard

The solar dynamo is a **chaotic, nonlinear** system. While the ~11-year periodicity is robust, the *amplitude* of each cycle varies dramatically. Key challenges:

1. **No perfect periodicity**: Cycle lengths range from 9 to 14 years, making seasonal modelling imprecise.
2. **Amplitude unpredictability**: Physical models of the solar dynamo still struggle to predict the strength of the next cycle years in advance.
3. **Stochastic bursts**: Individual flares and CMEs are essentially unpredictable more than a few days out.

State-of-the-art predictions combine statistical models with **physics-based solar dynamo simulations** and **precursor methods** (using polar magnetic field measurements to predict the next cycle's strength).
:::

```{python}
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scattergl(

    mode="markers", marker=dict(size=1.5, color=SOLAR_PRIMARY, opacity=0.2),
    name="Daily Sunspots", showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=1)
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=df_sorted["Date"], y=df_sorted["SSN_MA30"],
    mode="lines", line=dict(color=SOLAR_PRIMARY, width=2),
    name="Sunspot Number (30d MA)",
), row=1, col=1)

# Panel 2: Kp max
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scattergl(
    x=df_sorted["Date"], y=df_sorted["Estimated K Max"],
    mode="markers", marker=dict(size=1.5, color=GEO_PRIMARY, opacity=0.2),
    name="Daily Kp max", showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=2)
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=df_sorted["Date"], y=df_sorted["Kp_MA30"],
    mode="lines", line=dict(color=GEO_PRIMARY, width=2),
    name="Kp max (30d MA)",
), row=1, col=2)

# Panel 3: Flares stacked area
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=df_sorted["Date"], y=df_sorted["Flares_C_MA30"],
    mode="lines", line=dict(color=SOLAR_SECONDARY, width=1),
    fillcolor="rgba(255,210,63,0.4)",
    name="C-class (30d MA)", stackgroup="flares",
), row=2, col=1)
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=df_sorted["Date"], y=df_sorted["Flares_M_MA30"],
    mode="lines", line=dict(color=SOLAR_PRIMARY, width=1),
    fillcolor="rgba(255,107,53,0.5)",
    name="M-class (30d MA)", stackgroup="flares",
), row=2, col=1)
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=df_sorted["Date"], y=df_sorted["Flares_X_MA30"],
    mode="lines", line=dict(color=ALERT_COLOR, width=1),
    fillcolor="rgba(239,71,111,0.6)",
    name="X-class (30d MA)", stackgroup="flares",
), row=2, col=1)

# Panel 4: Radio Flux
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scattergl(
    x=df_sorted["Date"], y=df_sorted["Radio Flux 10.7cm"],
    mode="markers", marker=dict(size=1.5, color=SOLAR_SECONDARY, opacity=0.2),
    name="Daily F10.7", showlegend=False,
), row=2, col=2)
fig_dash.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=df_sorted["Date"], y=df_sorted["F107_MA30"],
    mode="lines", line=dict(color=SOLAR_SECONDARY, width=2),
    name="F10.7 (30d MA)",
), row=2, col=2)

# Synchronize x-axes and add range slider
fig_dash.update_xaxes(matches="x")
fig_dash.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True, row=2, col=2)

fig_dash.update_yaxes(title_text="Sunspot Number", row=1, col=1)
fig_dash.update_yaxes(title_text="Kp (max)", row=1, col=2)
fig_dash.update_yaxes(title_text="Flares / day (30d avg)", row=2, col=1)
fig_dash.update_yaxes(title_text="SFU", row=2, col=2)

fig_dash.update_layout(
    title="Space Weather Dashboard: Solar & Geomagnetic Activity (1997-2024)",
    height=800,
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=-0.15, xanchor="center", x=0.5, font=dict(size=10)),
    margin=dict(b=120),
)
fig_dash.show()
```

### Key Takeaways

- **The ~11-year solar cycle** is the dominant rhythm in nearly every variable --- sunspot numbers, radio flux, and flare rates all rise and fall in concert, though individual cycles differ substantially in amplitude.
- **Geomagnetic activity lags solar activity by 1--2 days** for flare-associated CME events, as confirmed by our superposed epoch analysis.
- **X-class flares are rare but impactful** --- they make up a tiny fraction of all flares yet produce the most severe geomagnetic storms.
- **Forecasting solar activity remains challenging**: While the periodic component is captured by SARIMA and Prophet, the chaotic nature of the solar dynamo limits predictability.
- **Multi-instrument monitoring is essential** --- no single index tells the whole story. The dashboard above shows how combining sunspot counts, radio flux, flare rates, and geomagnetic indices gives a far richer picture.
